user: Is unemployment insurance part of a federal program?
assistant: Yes, the Unemployment Insurance (UI) program can be considered part of a federal program because it is authorized by the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA). However, it is jointly funded by both the federal and state governments, and is administered at the state level. In California, the UI program is managed by the Unemployment Insurance Branch of the Employment Development Department (EDD).
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
How does it work?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
The Unemployment Insurance (UI) program provides weekly benefits to unemployed workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own. In California, this program is managed by the Unemployment Insurance Branch of the Employment Development Department (EDD). 
To qualify for benefits, a claimant must be able to work, actively seeking employment, and willing to accept a suitable job. The amount of benefits a claimant receives is based on their earnings during a specified "base period." The UI program is funded through unemployment tax contributions that employers pay for each covered worker. 
California law permits part-time employees to file a UI claim. The maximum weekly benefit is capped at $230 for up to 26 weeks. Unfortunately, benefit levels, which are determined by state law, have not been increased since 1992. 
The mission of the Unemployment Insurance Branch is to provide unemployment insurance services to workers and employers in California. This program serves as a short-term wage replacement for unemployed individuals and is funded by contributions from employers.
[The End of Reference Answer]

[The Start of Assistant's Answer]
According to page 1, Unemployment Insurance (UI) works as follows:
- It is a federal-state program authorized by federal law. States set benefit and employer contribution levels, and employer unemployment taxes finance it.
- To qualify, you must be able to work, seek work, and be willing to accept suitable work. California allows part-time employees to file claims.
- Benefits depend on earnings during your “base period.” The document lists California’s maximum as $230 weekly for 26 weeks.
- When certifying, report total earnings for the week worked. The greater of $25 or 25% of wages is not deducted; the remainder is.
- Excess earnings or inability/unavailability to work may make you ineligible that week; continue certifying for other weeks.
- Refusing work triggers a phone interview and employer contact. Refusing suitable work without good cause may affect eligibility.
[The End of Assistant's Answer]

[The Start of Document]
Able and available to work – If you said you were not able or available to work when you certified, you may not be eligible for benefits that week. Even if you are not eligible for benefits one week, you still may be eligible other weeks, so you should continue to certify.
Earnings – If you earned too much in a week, you may not be eligible for benefits that week. When certifying for regular unemployment benefits, you must report total earnings for the week you worked. The first $25 or 25% of your wages, whichever is more, will not be deducted from your benefit amount, but the rest will.
Suitable work – If you said you refused any work when you certified, we must schedule a phone interview to ask why. We will also contact the employer that offered you the job. If you refused to return to your job or other suitable work without good cause, you may not be eligible for benefits. To learn more about good cause, refer to Returning to Work.
